```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 6,
  out.width = "95%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```



# Problem 1
## Dataset description
```{r noaa-description}
data("ny_noaa")
noaa_dimensions <- dim(ny_noaa)
noaa_missingness <- ny_noaa |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "proportion_missing"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion_missing))
knitr::kable(
  noaa_missingness,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Variable", "Proportion missing"),
  caption = "Missingness in the NY NOAA dataset"
)
```


The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r scales::comma(noaa_dimensions[1])` observations and `r noaa_dimensions[2]` variables. Each row is a daily weather record from one weather station. The key variables are the station identifier (`id`), date, precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), minimum temperature (`tmin`), and maximum temperature (`tmax`). Missing data are a substantial concern: the highest missingness occurs in `r noaa_missingness$variable[1]`, for which `r scales::percent(noaa_missingness$proportion_missing[1], accuracy = 0.1)` of observations are missing. Any analysis based on these measures therefore uses only the available observations for the variables involved.
## Data cleaning and common snowfall values
```{r noaa-cleaning}
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-",
    convert = TRUE,
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  # reasonable units
  mutate(
    across(c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin), as.numeric),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = tmax / 10,
    tmin = tmin / 10
  )

common_snowfall =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, name = "number_of_days", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

knitr::kable(
  common_snowfall,
  col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Number of station-days"),
  caption = "Ten most commonly observed snowfall values"
)
```

I separated the date into numeric year, month, and day variables and converted precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature from tenths of their reported units to millimeters and degrees Celsius. The most common snowfall value is `r common_snowfall$snow[1]` mm, observed on `r scales::comma(common_snowfall$number_of_days[1])` station-days. This is expected because most days have no or little snowfall. Other frequent values are small amounts or values produced by standard measurement increments and rounding.

## Average January and July maximum tem
```{r noaa-January-July-plot}
monthly_station_temperature =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), 
    labels = c("January", "July"))
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(is.finite(mean_tmax))

ggplot(
  monthly_station_temperature,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, color = "green") +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average maximum temperature by station and year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```
The plot shows a strong and interpretable seasonal contrast: July maximum temperatures are much higher than January maximum temperatures. Stations generally follow similar long-term patterns, while the vertical spread reflects geographic differences among stations. A few station-years are separated sharply from the main collection of lines; these may represent unusual weather, incomplete monthly records, or measurement problems and should be checked before being treated as meaningful climate signals.


## Temperature relationship and snowfall distribution
```{r noaa-temperature-snowfall-plot}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily minimum and maximum temperatures",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = snow)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "blue", color = "white", scale = "width") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of positive snowfall below 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 6))

temperature_plot + snowfall_plot
```
The hexbin plot is preferable to a scatterplot because the dataset contains many overlapping observations. It shows a strong positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperature, with the greatest density near moderate temperatures and also some outliers on the edge of the plot. The yearly snowfall distributions are right-skewed: small positive snowfall amounts occur most often, while larger events below 100 mm are less common. The overall shape is broadly similar across years, although the upper tail and concentration vary from year to year.

## Problem 2


## Importing, tidying, and merging the NHANES data
```{r nhanes-import-clean}
nhanes_demographics =
  read_csv(
  "nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4,
  na = c("NA", ".", ""),
  show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

nhanes_activity =
  read_csv(
  "nhanes_accel.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))

nhanes_tidy =
  nhanes_demographics |>
  inner_join(nhanes_activity, by = "seqn")

nhanes_participants =
  nhanes_tidy |>
  distinct(seqn, .keep_all = TRUE)
```
After excluding participants younger than 21 and participants with missing demographic information, the analytic dataset contains `r n_distinct(nhanes_tidy$seqn)` participants and `r scales::comma(nrow(nhanes_tidy))` participant-minute observations. The long format preserves every demographic variable and every original minute-level MIMS value while making time-course summaries straightforward.


## Sex and education table and age distributions
```{r nhanes-demographic-summary}
sex_education_table =
  nhanes_participants |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(education)


knitr::kable(
  sex_education_table,
  caption = "Number of participants by education and sex"
)

ggplot(nhanes_participants, aes(x = age, fill = sex),colour = age) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by education and sex",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```
The table indicates that participants with more than a high school education form the largest education group in this analytic sample. The density curves also show that age composition differs by education level, so comparisons of activity across education categories should be interpreted with age in mind. Within each panel, the male and female distributions overlap substantially, although their peaks and tails are not identical.

## Total daily activity
```{r nhanes-total-activity}
participant_activity =
  nhanes_tidy |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(
  participant_activity,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity across age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Total activity generally declines with age, although there is considerable participant-level variation. The smooth curves suggest that the size and shape of the age-related decline differ across education groups and, in some panels, between men and women. Because these are descriptive smooths rather than adjusted estimates, apparent differences should not be interpreted as causal effects of sex or education.
## Twenty-four-hour activity profiles
```{r nhanes-activity-course}
activity_course =
  nhanes_tidy |>
  mutate(hour = minute / 60) |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute, hour) |>
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(activity_course, aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, span = 0.08, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average activity over a 24-hour day",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Activity is lowest overnight, rises rapidly in the morning, remains elevated through the daytime, and falls again in the evening. This shared daily rhythm is visible in all three education groups. Differences between men and women are smaller overnight and more noticeable during waking hours, while the timing and height of daytime peaks vary somewhat by education level.


# Problem 3
## Importing, cleaning, and describing the Citi Bike data
```{r citibike-import-clean}
citibike_files =
  tribble(
  ~file_name, ~year, ~month,
  "Jan 2020 Citi.csv", 2020, "January",
  "July 2020 Citi.csv", 2020, "July",
  "Jan 2024 Citi.csv", 2024, "January",
  "July 2024 Citi.csv", 2024, "July"
  )

citibike_data =
  citibike_files |>
  mutate(
    ride_data = map(
      file_name,
      ~ read_csv(file.path("citibike", .x), show_col_types = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(ride_data) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2020, 2024)),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("member", "casual"),
      labels = c("Member", "Casual")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic bike", "Electric bike")
    )
  )
```
The combined Citi Bike dataset contains `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike_data))` rides and `r ncol(citibike_data)` variables. Each row represents one sampled ride and includes a ride identifier, bike type, day of the week, duration in minutes, starting and ending station names, membership status, year, and month. The dataset combines January and July observations from 2020 and 2024, which supports comparisons across season and year.

## Ride counts by year, month, and membership status
```{r citibike-ride-counts}
ride_count_table =
  citibike_data |>
  count(year, month, member_casual, name = "number_of_rides") |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = number_of_rides,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(year, month)


knitr::kable(
  ride_count_table,
  caption = "Number of rides by year, month, and membership status"
)
```
Ride counts are higher in July than in January in both years, which is consistent with more favorable summer riding conditions. Members account for more rides than casual riders in every year-month combination. The sample also contains substantially more rides in 2024 than in 2020, reflecting the system's growth as well as the sampling design described in the assignment.
## Five most popular starting stations in July 2024
```{r citibike-popular-stations}
popular_stations =
  citibike_data |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July", !is.na(start_station_name)) |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "number_of_rides", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

knitr::kable(
  popular_stations,
  col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"),
  caption = "Five most popular starting stations in July 2024"
)
```
The most popular starting station in July 2024 is `r popular_stations$start_station_name[1]`, with `r scales::comma(popular_stations$number_of_rides[1])` rides in the sample. The leading stations are concentrated at locations that plausibly generate heavy recreational or commuter traffic, although this table describes trip origins rather than the number of unique riders.


## Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year
```{r citibike-median-duration}
median_duration =
  citibike_data |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


ggplot(
  median_duration,
  aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year",
    x = "Day of week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
Median rides are generally longer in July than in January, especially on weekends, which suggests a larger recreational component during summer. Weekday medians are comparatively stable and shorter, consistent with more routine transportation. Comparing the two panels also shows whether the weekly pattern changed between 2020 and 2024 without obscuring the seasonal contrast.


## Ride duration in 2024 by month, membership, and bike type
```{r citibike-2024-duration-distribution}
citibike_data |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
    trim = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.14,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Classic bike" = "#74A9CF", "Electric bike" = "#F03B20")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of ride duration in 2024",
    subtitle = "The display is limited to 0–60 minutes so the central distributions are readable.",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )
```
Casual riders tend to take longer trips than members, particularly in July. Electric-bike rides are generally more concentrated at shorter durations than classic-bike rides, which may reflect faster travel or different use cases. July distributions are wider and have higher centers than January distributions, especially for casual riders. The y-axis restriction changes only the displayed range; it does not remove observations from the computation of the violin and boxplot summaries.
